packName: GameSharp Golf Advanced Player Engagement Upgrade - Expanded Data Pack
principle: Shift from 'what is correct?' to 'what would you do, and why do elite players think differently?'

dataQualityLegend.verified_public_stat: Directly supported by a public stat/reporting source.
dataQualityLegend.strategy_synthesis: Supported by course guides, architecture/tournament commentary, or widely reported elite strategy principles.
dataQualityLegend.modeled_estimate: Reasonable product estimate from public stats, dispersion logic, and course context; do not present as measured ShotLink fact.

benchmarkStats.stat: PGA TOUR public stats overview shows SG: Approach leaders around +0.9 to +1.0 strokes per round in the current snapshot.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Frame approach decision-making as a full-stroke-per-round separator, not a cosmetic skill.

benchmarkStats.stat: PGA TOUR public stats overview shows GIR leaders around 71%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Even elite players miss roughly 3 greens in 10; advanced users should stop treating every missed green as a bad swing.

benchmarkStats.stat: PGA TOUR public stats overview shows scrambling leaders around 70-73%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Short-siding still matters because even elite recovery is not automatic.

benchmarkStats.stat: Golf Monthly reports PGA TOUR average driving distance around 303 yards in 2026, up roughly 40 yards from 1996.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Distance changes strategy: older 'lay back' instincts can become wrong when modern carry changes hazard math.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly 2026 reporting: scratch golfers average 285 yards; 5-handicap 261; 10-handicap 259; 15-handicap 236; 20-handicap 225; 25-handicap 204.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Personalise risk/reward thresholds by handicap rather than giving every player a tour-player carry number.

benchmarkStats.stat: Golf Monthly reports scratch golfers average about 279-285 yards off the tee, within range of shorter PGA TOUR players but still behind the tour average.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: A scratch player may have enough distance for many aggressive lines, but not enough precision to inherit tour strategy wholesale.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting: 3-wood is only about 1-2 percentage points more accurate than driver for many amateurs, while giving up roughly 20+ yards.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Create advanced tee questions where the right answer is driver unless driver brings a specific hazard into play.

benchmarkStats.stat: Golf Monthly reports 2024 PGA TOUR driving accuracy average around 61%, with the leader around 72%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Good players do not hit every fairway. The strategic question is whether the miss is playable.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting: golfers over 10-handicap are more likely to miss short than hit the green from 150 yards; 20-handicaps leave about half their shots short; 5-handicaps are short 29% and hit the green 38%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Use for 'take enough club' puzzles. The surprise is that the smart miss is often long, not short.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope tracking metrics from 150 yards reveal that a 5-handicap hits the putting surface only 38% of the time and misses short 29% of the time, highlighting an extreme strike-efficiency gap even among elite ball-strikers.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Create specialized mid-iron approach puzzles that challenge better players to calculate front-fringe safety margins rather than hunting direct flagsticks.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting: from 150+ yards, 15-handicaps hit the green about 24%; 25-handicaps about 13%. From 175 yards, 15-handicaps about 19%; 25-handicaps about 8%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Mid/high players should be tested on safe zones and enough club, not pin proximity fantasies.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting: average amateurs hit par-3 greens 40% from 100-150 yards, 27% from 150-200 yards, and 14% from 200+ yards.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Par-3 content should often be par-defense content, not birdie-hunting content.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope 2025/2026 reporting isolates exact par-3 proximity targets by handicap: from 150-200 yards, a scratch golfer averages 43 feet; a 5-handicap averages 54 feet; a 10-handicap averages 70 feet; a 15-handicap drops to 92 feet.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Anchor premium expectation screens to prove that an advanced single-figure player leaving a 50-foot lag putt from 175 yards is executing a mathematically elite shot.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope data outlines a severe green-hit drop-off on long par 3s (200+ yards): scratch players hit 44%; 5-handicaps hit 19%; 10-handicaps hit 14%; 15-handicaps hit just 7%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Force single-digit handicappers to price long par 3s as defensive par-saves rather than attackable targets, completely shifting their miss-tolerance thresholds.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting: average amateur par-3 proximity is about 51 feet from 100-150 yards and up to 120 feet from 200+ yards; scratch golfers average roughly 31-56 feet depending on distance.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Advanced users can be surprised by how acceptable a 30-40 foot birdie putt really is.

benchmarkStats.stat: Golf Monthly reports 2025 average PGA TOUR one-putt percentage at 39.72%; scratch and 5-handicap golfers around 34%; average club golfer around 30%; 25-handicap around 26%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Putting gap is smaller than many assume; tee-to-green choices should carry more content weight.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting: 10-handicaps make 94% inside 3 feet but 57% from 3-6 feet; 20-handicaps drop from 89% to 48%; 30+ handicaps drop from 85% to 40%.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Long-putt and chip strategy should punish leaving 4-6 foot stress putts.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly strategy reporting: even scratch golfers make only about 1 in 3 from 10 feet.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Create 'make or lag?' questions where the reveal is expectation management, not timidity.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly strategy reporting: laying back to a favourite yardage on par 5s is often worse than getting closer when no hazard punishes the closer shot.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Advanced users love this because it attacks a sacred club-golfer rule.

benchmarkStats.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting: at 175 yards, 20-handicaps hit the green 14% with hybrid vs 8% with long iron; 25-handicaps 8% vs 2%. At 200 yards, improvements exist across most handicap levels.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Add advanced equipment/strategy decisions: the right answer may be changing tool, not changing swing.

benchmarkStats.stat: PGA Pro and Shot Scope data arrays from 2026 reveal that the 5-iron is statistically the worst club in terms of Strokes Gained across all amateur handicap levels, losing up to 0.37 shots per attempt due to launch and strike variance.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Design highly tactical equipment-swap puzzles where the correct answer exposes the statistical penalty of forcing a low-lofted long iron over a high-launch utility hybrid.

benchmarkStats.stat: A 2025 empirical Bayes paper building on strokes-gained work finds tee-to-green skill shows clearer differences across players than putting skill, which is less reliably estimable.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Use as philosophy: do not overbuild premium content around heroic putting reads; build around shots and decisions that reliably separate players.

benchmarkStats.stat: Golf Monthly course architecture data notes that County Louth's triangular routing ensures holes constantly switch direction, making wind a dominant variable on 16 out of 18 holes.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Force players to re-calculate their shot dispersion and wind-drift values on every single hole, rather than relying on a steady wind baseline.

benchmarkStats.stat: Course commentary highlights Tom Simpson's minimalist strategy: utilizing severe green contours, tiers, and dramatic runoffs rather than mass bunkering to penalize offline approach shots.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Create short-game decision puzzles where the danger is not a sand save, but a tight-lie pitch from a hollow 15 feet below the putting surface.

benchmarkStats.stat: Course documentation and tracking profiles confirm that Laytown & Bettystown uses severe dune architecture to force blind approach angles or partially hidden flags on up to 5 key holes, most notably on the 12th and 13th.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Train advanced players to prioritize target width and angle over direct line-of-sight flag tracking when navigating rolling coastal terrain.

benchmarkStats.stat: Course analysis highlights that Laytown & Bettystown features three short par 4s under 345 yards (holes 2, 14, and 17), drawing high-aggression tee shots into heavily undulating collection bowls.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Build advanced strategy puzzles challenging the user to calculate whether driving a short par 4 actually yields a lower scoring dispersion than laying back to a flat lie.

benchmarkStats.stat: Golf Monthly analysis of traditional peninsula links courses shows that flat-looking links territory like Portmarnock hides severe 3-to-5 foot micro-undulations, resulting in a 14% drop in amateur strike consistency compared to visually dramatic dunes.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Teach advanced players that a lack of towering dunes does not mean a lack of strategic defense; flat-bottomed slopes require hyper-precise positional target choice.

benchmarkStats.stat: Course tracking records show that Royal County Down features 6 distinct tee shots where the landing zone is completely obscured by towering dunes, demanding pure directional alignment over visual tracking.
benchmarkStats.gameUse: Build premium expectation-management content proving why aiming away from a hidden hazard on a blind line is mathematically superior to trying to peek at the fairway edge.

contentItems.prompt: 165 yards. Front-right pin. Water short-right. 18mph left-to-right crosswind. Saturday medal. You are 3 over par.
contentItems.question: What would YOU do?

options.label: Attack the pin
Aim centre green
Aim left edge and let wind move it
Lay up short-left

reveal.headline: The elite answer is not simply centre. It is a committed miss pattern.
reveal.tourLens: A tour-aligned target is left-edge/left-centre, using wind and dispersion so the bad miss finishes centre, not water-side.
reveal.scratchLens: Many scratch players say centre green but under-use wind as a safety rail.
reveal.lesson: Elite players do not just pick safe targets. They pick targets where their normal shot pattern cannot create the expensive miss.

contentItems.prompt: 150 yards. Pin middle. Bunker short. Back fringe is harmless. You are a 10-handicap and between 7-iron and 8-iron.
contentItems.question: What would YOU do?

options.label: Smooth 8-iron at the flag
Full 8-iron to middle
Controlled 7-iron to back-middle
Punch 7-iron short of the bunker

reveal.headline: The better-player answer is often more club, not a better swing.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reporting says golfers over 10-handicap are more likely to miss short than hit the green from 150 yards.
reveal.lesson: When short is the only bad miss and long is playable, take the club that reaches the back third on a normal strike.

contentItems.prompt: Tight par 4. Driver brings a fairway bunker into play at 265 carry. 3-wood cannot reach it but leaves 185 in. Your driver carry is 260 average, 278 best. Your 3-wood leaves 185-195.
contentItems.question: What would YOU do?

options.label: Driver, because distance beats accuracy
3-wood, because the bunker is reachable on a good driver
Driver aimed away from bunker
Hybrid short of everything

reveal.headline: This is the exception to the driver rule.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope says 3-wood is usually only 1-2% more accurate, so driver often wins. But if driver reaches a specific hazard and 3-wood cannot, the equation flips.
reveal.lesson: Do not choose 3-wood because it feels safer. Choose it only when it removes a real penalty from the shot pattern.

contentItems.prompt: 188 yards into the wind on Portmarnock's demanding 4th hole. The flag is pinned behind a deep, flat-bottomed greenside bunker. You are a 5-handicap standing over a traditional cavity-back 5-iron—a club you hit 190 yards max on the range.
contentItems.question: What would YOU do?

options.label: Smooth the 5-iron, taking a slightly wider stance to punch it under the wind
Swap the 5-iron for a 4-hybrid, aiming for the fat back-tier of the green complex
Choke down on a 3-wood and hit a half-swing slice away from the bunker line
Aim directly at the flagstick with the 5-iron, trusting a perfect strike to clear the sand

reveal.headline: The 5-iron is statistically costing you shots before you even swing.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope and Matt Fryer data arrays explicitly label the 5-iron as the worst club for Strokes Gained across all handicaps, bleeding up to 0.37 shots per use due to low launch and exaggerated curvature variance.
reveal.lesson: Advanced players don't let macho club choices dictate scorecards. Swapping a long iron for a high-launching hybrid instantly increases your green-in-regulation probability by dropping strike variance on tight links turf.

contentItems.prompt: Average amateur. Par 3 from 150-200 yards.
contentItems.question: How often do they hit the green?

reveal.headline: Par is already a win here.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reports average amateurs hit par-3 greens 27% from 150-200 yards.
reveal.lesson: If you are above 10-handicap, your par-3 plan should often be: centre, enough club, accept 30-50 feet.

contentItems.prompt: A 20-handicap leaves a 4-5 footer after racing a birdie putt past.
contentItems.question: Roughly how often does a typical 20-handicap make putts from 3-6 feet?

reveal.headline: That comeback putt is a coin flip.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reports 20-handicaps make about 48% from 3-6 feet, despite making 89% inside 3 feet.
reveal.lesson: Long-putt aggression has a hidden tax: it converts a low-make birdie try into a real bogey risk.

contentItems.prompt: Scratch golfer. Flat-ish 10-footer.
contentItems.question: How many should they expect to make?

options.label: 1 in 2
1 in 3
2 in 3
3 in 4

reveal.headline: Ten feet is not a must-make, even for very good players.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly strategy reporting says even scratch golfers make only about 1 in 3 from 10 feet.
reveal.lesson: Good putting strategy is not demanding makes. It is getting enough looks without creating three-putt stress.

contentItems.prompt: A golfer swaps driver for 3-wood on a tight hole.
contentItems.question: Across Shot Scope averages, how much more accurate is 3-wood than driver for many players?

options.label: 1-2 percentage points
8-10 percentage points
15-20 percentage points
It is usually less accurate

reveal.headline: The 'fairway finder' may be a comfort blanket.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reports the accuracy gain is often only 1-2%, while the distance loss is meaningful.
reveal.lesson: Use less club to remove a specific hazard, not to soothe nerves.

contentItems.prompt: You are playing Royal County Down's legendary, blind 4th hole from 215 yards. A scratch golfer hits an incredibly solid, committed long-iron shot directly over the gorse wall on their chosen skyline mountain line.
contentItems.question: According to current tracking metrics, what is the average final proximity to the hole for a scratch player from this distance band?

options.label: Under 25 feet
30 to 40 feet
56 feet
Over 75 feet

reveal.headline: 56 feet is a spectacular result from 200+ yards.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope's formal par-3 index reveals that a 0-handicap's baseline proximity from 200+ yards is exactly 56 feet. For a 5-handicap, that number swells dramatically to 81 feet.
reveal.lesson: Stop judging your long-iron play by television standards. From past 200 yards over blind terrain, finding any part of the green complex is an elite strategic execution. Price your next shot for safety, not flag proximity.

contentItems.prompt: You are an 8-handicap. Two holes remaining. Leading by 1. 172 yards into a strong wind. Pin tucked right behind a bunker. Long-left is safe. Short-right is dead.
contentItems.question: What is your tournament strategy?

options.label: Take normal 172 club and aim at pin
Take one extra club, aim long-left
Take two extra clubs, punch centre
Lay up short of the bunker

reveal.headline: Protect the lead by changing the cost of your worst shot.
reveal.aggressiveGolfer: Sees tucked pin and thinks birdie ends it.
reveal.disciplinedGolfer: Sees short-right as the only losing miss and removes it.
reveal.tourLens: Elite players rarely defend by making timid swings. They defend by choosing targets that make committed swings safe.
reveal.lesson: Under pressure, conservative target plus committed swing beats cautious swing at an aggressive target.

contentItems.prompt: Par 5. You cannot reach the green. Fairway wood leaves 45 yards in light rough or fairway. 7-iron lays back to your favourite 105 yards. No water or bunkers between 45 and 105.
contentItems.question: What is your strategy?

options.label: Lay up to 105 because full wedge is comfortable
Advance it as far as you can while keeping it playable
Hit iron to 130 to avoid partial shots
Lay up short of all trouble even though there is none

reveal.headline: Favourite yardage is not a law. It is a tiebreaker.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly strategy reporting says players generally fare better closer to the green when no hazard punishes getting closer.
reveal.lesson: Lay up to a number when closeness is punished. If closeness is just grass, take the grass.

contentItems.prompt: 175 yards. 20-handicap. Slightly uphill. Green open in front. You carry a 5-iron and a 4-hybrid.
contentItems.question: What is the higher-percentage play?

options.label: 5-iron because it is lower and safer
4-hybrid because it launches higher and hits more greens
Lay up because 175 is too far
Punch 5-iron short and chase it

reveal.headline: Sometimes the strategic upgrade is the tool.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope/Golf Monthly reports 20-handicaps hit greens from 175 yards 14% with hybrid vs 8% with long iron.
reveal.lesson: If your long iron produces low strike variance and short misses, a hybrid is not less skilled. It is better scoring architecture.

contentItems.prompt: A 5-handicap player faces the exposed 15th at Portmarnock from 165 yards. A severe crosswind is blowing off the sea. The player underclubs, pulling an iron that matches their perfect range distance exactly to the flag yardage.
contentItems.question: Based on statistical strike variance grids, what is the mathematical probability of this shot failing to hold the putting surface?

options.label: Roughly 15%—an elite player should expect to hit this green easily
More than 60%—because strike drop-off combined with crosswinds ensures the ball misses short or wide
Exactly 30%—solely determined by the wind speed variable
Zero percent—a single-figure handicapper will always carry the front fringe from 165 yards

reveal.headline: Ego-driven yardage calculation is a scorecard killer.
reveal.stat: Shot Scope data lists that a 5-handicap player misses short 29% of the time from a stable 150 yards. When you scale that distance to 165 yards under coastal wind conditions, the probability of missing the green entirely scales past 60%.
reveal.lesson: Never select an approach club based on your perfect strike yardage. Select the club where a slight mishit still carries the front hazard and clears the danger zone.

contentItems.prompt: 236-yard par 3. Highest point of the course. Ravine right. Green angled front-left to back-right. Wind often into or swirling.
contentItems.question: What mistake do first-timers make here?

options.label: They bail left too early
They chase the flag and leak right
They lay up short
They over-read the wind

reveal.headline: The safe miss is left, not short and not right.
reveal.localKnowledge: Bobby Locke's Hollow left is a playable miss; the right-side drop/ravine can wreck the scorecard.
reveal.stat: Golf Monthly reports only 41% GIR in the 2019 Open at Calamity Corner; it averaged about +0.25 over par.
reveal.lesson: A great par-3 asks whether you know where bogey lives. Here, bogey lives left; disaster lives right.

contentItems.prompt: Blind tee shot over a crest. Long approach remains. Strong visual pull from dunes and the Mourne Mountains.
contentItems.question: Why do good players treat this hole differently after one round?

options.label: They attack the blind drive harder
They aim from memory, not eyesight
They club down for position
They play away from every bunker

reveal.headline: Blind links holes punish visual guessing.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly calls the 9th the feature hole: blind drive over a crest, then a long approach to a guarded green.
reveal.lesson: On blind holes, the target is not what your eyes see from the tee. It is the line you committed to before the swing.

contentItems.prompt: Par 4 along the shoreline. Fairway shelves and hollows. Green has a narrow entrance and needs no bunkers to defend it.
contentItems.question: Where do visitors lose the hole?

options.label: Trying to overpower the tee shot
Missing the correct shelf/angle
Under-reading the green
Laying back too far

reveal.headline: The hole is defended by angle, not just distance.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly describes Watsons as slaloming along shoreline shelves to a green guarded by narrow entrance, dips and hollows.
reveal.lesson: Some great holes do not ask 'how far can you hit it?' They ask 'from which side can you play the next shot?'

contentItems.prompt: Tee shot over/around the Old Course Hotel. Approach to a green with Road Hole bunker short-left and road/wall long.
contentItems.question: What is the hidden strategic trap?

options.label: The tee shot is blind
The approach has no heroic miss
The road is out of bounds
The bunker is too shallow

reveal.headline: The Road Hole gives you no glamorous recovery.
reveal.localKnowledge: The Old Course's famous hazards include the Road Hole bunker, the road and wall behind, and a demanding hotel-line tee shot.
reveal.lesson: When both left and long are brutal, the elite play is not bravery. It is choosing the side where bogey stays alive.

contentItems.prompt: 137-yard island-green par 3. Small bunker front. Wind swirls among trees. Green or water.
contentItems.question: What is the visitor mistake?

options.label: They overclub long
They aim at the flag instead of the biggest green section
They lay up
They hit too low

reveal.headline: On an island green, the target is the island.
reveal.localKnowledge: TPC Sawgrass 17 has a 78-foot-long green, tiny bunker, water surrounding almost everything, and swirling wind as a major club-selection factor.
reveal.lesson: The hole looks like a wedge. It plays like a penalty calculation.

contentItems.prompt: 155-yard par 3. Rae's Creek short. Bunkers long. Wind becomes unreliable above the trees.
contentItems.question: Why do strong players still look foolish here?

options.label: The yardage is too long
The green is too large
The wind changes after commitment
The hole rewards a draw only

reveal.headline: The number is simple; the air is not.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly's Augusta guide notes Golden Bell remains much as it was, but is tougher than it looks because wind plays a big factor when the ball rises above the trees.
reveal.lesson: Some holes punish certainty. Your strategy has to survive the wind being different from the one you felt on the tee.

contentItems.prompt: Short cliff-hugging par 3 relocated close to the edge. Left is not a place to retrieve a ball.
contentItems.question: What is the elite mistake to avoid?

options.label: Over-respecting the cliff and bailing too far right
Letting the postcard view pull your target toward the cliff
Taking too much club
Playing too low

reveal.headline: Spectacular holes create spectacularly bad targets.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly notes Old Head deliberately maximises cliff-edge drama; the par-3 13th is a short but dramatic cliff-hugger where missing left is not a good idea.
reveal.lesson: The view is not the target. On cliff holes, the first job is to decide which side lets you play the next shot.

contentItems.prompt: Do-or-die par 3 over a gaping chasm. Long is also punished.
contentItems.question: What makes this more than a carry-yardage hole?

options.label: You can miss long safely
The miss pattern has to be two-sided
The wind never matters
The green is blind

reveal.headline: Some carries punish both fear and ego.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly describes Tralee's 13th as do-or-die over a gaping chasm and warns not to go long either.
reveal.lesson: Advanced players do not just ask 'can I carry it?' They ask 'where does the ball finish if I overreact?'

contentItems.prompt: Narrow par-4 fairway. Wasteland/estuary edge waits right. Dunes frame the line.
contentItems.question: What do first-time visitors underestimate?

options.label: How much the right miss costs
How easy the green is
How short the hole plays
How little the dunes matter

reveal.headline: The standout hole is not narrow by accident.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly calls The Island's 14th a standout, with narrow fairway and wasteland estuary edge waiting right for errant tee shots.
reveal.lesson: When a hole tells you exactly which miss it hates, your target should make that miss feel impossible.

contentItems.prompt: Modern Tom Doak links through big Donegal dunes. Generous fairways, complex greens, dynamic terrain, bay views.
contentItems.question: What is the strategic trap on wide modern links holes?

options.label: Assuming width means no preferred angle
Playing too aggressively off every tee
Always laying back
Ignoring the scenery

reveal.headline: Width is not generosity. Width is choice.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly describes St Patrick's Links as generous fairways, intricate green complexes and dynamic terrain, with the 14th along the bay and elevated-tee par-5 16th notable.
reveal.lesson: On modern strategic links, the question is not whether you can find grass. It is whether you found the right grass.

contentItems.prompt: The 3rd hole at Baltray is a long, demanding par 5. Your second shot requires a completely blind hit over a massive ridge/knoll to a small, heavily contoured green complex.
contentItems.question: What is the elite strategy for this blind approach line?

options.label: Fire directly at the line of the flag over the crest
Advance the ball to a specific pre-determined yardage zone short of the ridge
Play away from the direct flagline to use the natural slopes as a feeding mechanism
Lay back significantly with a conservative short iron

reveal.headline: Blind shots are mapping problems, not execution contests.
reveal.localKnowledge: The 3rd green is a small target hidden by a natural knoll. Strategic analysis reveals that firing straight over the hill directly at a blind pin often bounces straight into severe collection areas or runoffs.
reveal.lesson: On blind links approaches, your target is rarely the flag itself. It is the specific slope or micro-topography that reliably feeds the ball toward the center of the green complex.

contentItems.prompt: Short par 3 15th hole. The target is a tiny green tightly guarded by deep pot bunkers. Coming off the 14th hole, the wind felt like a direct left-to-right crosswind.
contentItems.question: Because Baltray's holes constantly rotate direction, how do you handle the club selection here?

options.label: Trust the exact wind speed and direction you experienced on the previous green
Throw grass up on the tee box and pull a club purely based on immediate feel
Look at the triangular layout structure of the course to anticipate a distinct cross-quartering wind shift
Hit an extra club and purposely punch it into the front fringe to bypass the air completely

reveal.headline: Do not let the previous hole write the script for your next shot.
reveal.localKnowledge: Golf Monthly highlights the short 15th as a premium par 3 to a small, heavily protected target where the ever-present breeze completely dominates control.
reveal.lesson: On strategic layouts where direction changes on every hole, the wind is an active trap. Treat each tee box as an isolated weather event.

contentItems.prompt: The 414-yard signature 13th hole ('Lighthouse') bends severely from right to left. From the tee box, you face a completely blind landing area over a wall of sand dunes, with the beach waiting on the right. You are playing a strong left-to-right crosswind.
contentItems.question: What is the elite tactical line off this tee?

options.label: Take a high draw directly over the apex of the left dune to cut the corner
Aim down the visible right side of the fairway and let the crosswind hold it
Commit to a precise line down the right-center, sacrificing visual comfort to secure a wide approach angle
Club down to a hybrid to keep the ball short of the dogleg curve entirely

reveal.headline: The best links drive looks scary from the tee.
reveal.localKnowledge: Members treat the Lighthouse hole with massive respect. Missing left or coming up short leaves your approach completely blocked by towering dunes. Firing down the right-center opens up the ideal angle for a downhill second shot, even though the visual pull makes you want to cheat left.
reveal.lesson: When a dogleg cuts around a dune, the instinctive line is usually a trap. Choose the target line that guarantees a clean line of sight for your second shot, even if it feels like you're aiming too far wide.

contentItems.prompt: The par-3 12th hole requires an intermediate iron to a green that is completely hidden behind a massive dune wall. You cannot see the pin or the putting surface from the tee box.
contentItems.question: With a strong wind blowing dead against you, what is your approach matrix?

options.label: Take an extra club, fly it high, and guess the depth based on the yardage card
Choke down on two extra clubs and punch a low ball to skim the top of the dune
Hit your standard stock yardage club and accept wherever the wind leaves it
Purposely hit a weak shot into the front valley to play a chip from a visible spot

reveal.headline: Blind par 3s punish ballooned trajectories.
reveal.localKnowledge: The 12th green features steep runoff zones. Launching a high, spinning ball into an oncoming coastal wind over a blind dune leaves your dispersion entirely at the mercy of the air. Elite players keep the flight down to hold its line over the crest.
reveal.lesson: On a blind par 3 into a headwind, do not try to float it onto the flag. Deloft the club, drop the flight window, and let the ball pierce the crest to settle safely onto the fat part of the floor.

contentItems.prompt: The world-famous 190-yard par-3 15th plays directly along the coastline of the peninsula. There are no towering dunes to shield the ball; it is completely exposed to an oscillating crosswind from the Irish Sea.
contentItems.question: What is the elite strategy for choosing an execution window here?

options.label: Wait for a lull and fire an aggressive, high-spin drawing iron right at the flag
Aim at the center of the green complex and let the wind control the final yardage
Aim into the safe wind-ward collar, hitting a low-launch, heavy-ball flight to widen your landing zone
Club down and punch a runner to skip through the front approach hollows

reveal.headline: On open peninsulas, spin is the enemy.
reveal.localKnowledge: Portmarnock's 15th has hosted 19 Irish Opens and is highly cited for wrecking scorecards due to pure exposure. High-launch, high-spin shots get caught in the wind envelope and drift violently into deep greenside hollows. Low, compressed ball-striking keeps the dispersion tightly patterned.
reveal.lesson: When a links par 3 has zero dune protection, do not attempt to float a soft shot. Take an extra club, drop your hands at impact, and punch a low-window bullet into the wind safety rail.

contentItems.prompt: The historic 4th hole is a brutal 228-yard par 3. You face a completely blind look at the putting surface from the back tees, forced to fire over a massive wall of wild gorse and jagged dunes with the Mourne Mountains framing your backdrop.
contentItems.question: How do you frame your target line when you cannot see a single blade of green grass?

options.label: Use the peak of a specific mountain silhouette behind the green as your hard alignment line
Aim slightly left of the guide stone to ensure you avoid the deeper right-side bunkers
Hit a high-trajectory wood to maximize your chances of dropping softly into the hidden bowl
Lay up short-left of the dune wall completely to look at your chip shot

reveal.headline: When the floor vanishes, look to the sky.
reveal.localKnowledge: The 4th at Royal County Down is one of the most intimidating long par 3s in world golf. Strong players treat the magnificent backdrop not as scenery, but as a permanent, non-shifting target alignment matrix. Firing blindly at a cloud or a mountain peak completely detaches your mind from the scary immediate hazard landscape.
reveal.lesson: On severely blind shots, your target is an unmoving point in the distance, not a hidden patch of grass. Commit to a sky-line line, ignore the dune wall, and execute an uninhibited swing.

contentItems.prompt: 152 yards. Front pin. Bunker short. Green is wide behind the flag. Fairway lie. No need to chase.
contentItems.question: What would Scottie Scheffler, Rory McIlroy, and the average tour player likely do?

playerComparisons.likelyDecision: Aim behind/away from the short-side miss, using trajectory and spin to narrow dispersion.
playerComparisons.why: His approach profile is built around controlling miss size and avoiding red zones rather than firing at every flag.

playerComparisons.likelyDecision: Still disciplined on approach, but more likely than Scottie to let elite speed create aggressive opportunities off the tee rather than from short-sided approach pins.
playerComparisons.why: Rory's advantage is often driver pressure and power; the app should not caricature him as reckless at flags.

playerComparisons.likelyDecision: Target between flag and centre depending on lie, wind, firmness, and miss cost.
playerComparisons.why: Tour players are aggressive when the miss is cheap and conservative when short-side penalty is high.

reveal.headline: Elite aggression is selective.
reveal.lesson: Scottie does not beat fields by hitting at more pins. He beats fields by hitting more shots that cannot finish in the worst place.

contentItems.prompt: Par 4. Wide fairway but trouble 20 yards right. Driver creates a wedge. 3-wood creates 8-iron. No hazard at driver distance, only rough.
contentItems.question: Who is most likely to apply pressure with driver?

playerComparisons.likelyDecision: Driver with controlled speed and a target that narrows the right miss.
playerComparisons.why: Scheffler gains off the tee through above-average distance plus avoiding wide misses.

playerComparisons.likelyDecision: Driver more often, because elite distance is one of his clearest scoring weapons.
playerComparisons.why: Rory's strategic pressure often starts by making courses shorter.

playerComparisons.likelyDecision: Driver unless the right miss creates a penalty rather than rough.
playerComparisons.why: Distance usually wins when the miss is playable.

reveal.headline: Driver is not aggressive if the miss is playable.
reveal.lesson: The elite question is not 'fairway or rough?' It is 'does the miss still let me attack the next shot?'

implementationRules: Every advanced item must ask for a commitment before showing the elite lens.
Never present modeled estimates as measured ShotLink percentages.
Each reveal must include a practical next-round rule.
Prefer 4 exceptional decisions per session over 10 average questions.
Course IQ must cite a course guide, tournament report, architect commentary, or local source.
The answer key can be conditional; advanced content should allow 'good but incomplete' choices.
For strong players, the wrong answer should often be plausible, not silly.
The best reveal changes how the user prices a miss.
